title: How is American Fiction not guilty of what it's critiquing?

commenti.body: I thought that was the point? The twist is we've been watching Monk's movie the whole time. None of that family stuff actually happened to him, that was just the award baity drama that the producer made him include.
Wait you're telling me that all of the movie was just monk's script all upto the point where he and the director are discussing the final scene.?
A la Adaptation?

That's what I thought the ending meant. And to those of us who nodded along with the suicide and the Alzheimer's and the closeted son, the twist kind of puts us on trial. "This melodrama seemed real and important to you, didn't it? That makes you just like the fans of *Fuck*!"

I don't believe that it is meant to be perceived as "black trauma porn" - it's "Hollywood trauma porn" and absolute awards bait.

I don't think the film is strong enough visually or within its overall production to make this concept fully fly, but it is full of admirable intent.

It is also vital for us to see black lives rendered and considered in such a predominantly white Hollywood way.

If anything the film should have been more critical of how stupid this type of storytelling is, but in order to appeal to that wide demographic the movie has to exist for them to.

It's a wild trick, not wholly successful for a more involved crowd but certainly seems likely to tickle the fancy of most mainstream audiences.

Some gay men may feel that they need their own version of American Fiction in which the self-hating and financially stricken protagonist writes an ostensibly satirical novel in which gay men are never not hanging around in underpants, taking drugs and being overtly camp.
This is wrong cos he says the real life Coraline didn't take him back

First, I read recently that the book the script was based on was from 2001 which would make it more relevant to that time frame. Secondly I think the whole thought bubble you’ve gone into is part of what is drawn attention to in the film. What is a black film or a black writer or a black director? As someone who isn’t black or white and isn’t American I think it’s interesting how things are qualified and examined. The US wrangles with identity in so many ways and it’s interesting to me. It’s very self referential and I think it does that well.

>Thus, American Fiction's only gripe really is with low-brow blaxploitation, not high-brow blaxploitation, which is definitely not what it set out to argue.

That is the point of view of the main character not the film. He believes that those stories reinforce stereotypes that should be ignored. I think the film is very critical of his snobbery. 

His view is challenged when he argues with Issa Rae's character. Her counterpoint is that those stories deserve to be told, and the white reception to those works reflect more on the audience than it does on the writers. She is not critical of his novel because of its genre. She sees how little research went into it and senses the superficiality that white authors missed.

But then the film has no point..? And you’re giving them more credit than they deserve. I don’t think they thought it through. That family story was made earnestly without a hint of satire. Even those who love the film don’t take it that way.

Well he didn't make up EVERYTHING. There really was a book *Fuck*, and we see here there really was a Coraline. He also really has a brother. But we don't know how much else of what we've seen is accurate to his life. 

Nothing from the Coraline subplot, incidentally, qualifies as awards bait or melodrama. It's a very normal, unremarkable relationship (until the running-to-her-front-door part, which we're told explicitly didn't happen.)

I’ve just seen it once, but I understood the line that the real girlfriend won’t return his call signals everything actually happened up to the point where he called the director in the hallway with an idea for a different movie. Which wasn’t the fake book he bought, but the making of the fake book. That’s when the movie and the movie within the movie diverged. 

But yes, there’s a rug pull and we have to consider the unreliable narrative, but I’m not clear it’s all fake.

It seems a bit odd that the film should call out awards bait by name while also including so many awards bait elements. Is that just coincidence? The family plot contains more separate awards bait elements than most straight-up award winning films.

If that’s the director’s intention then he either failed to convey that well? Or it’s a case of “jokes on you. I was only pretending to be an r-word.” Because this movie is begging us to care about his dumb family for 1 hour of the 2 hour running time then he wants to turn it into a joke, and one supposedly at our expense, because supposedly we’re dumb and enough to be interested in this crap?

Either way its not good.
I honestly think it included “awards bait elements” to actually get those awards. You have the correct interpretation of the film, but not the director’s intention.

I guess it’s only fair to say that i’m lost in the metaphors. You along with many commenters here made it clear the film’s perspective and the main character’s perspective don’t particularly align. But im still lost as to what the point is? At best it’s a jumbled message, at worst it’s contradictory and obtuse.

>At best it’s a jumbled message, at worst it’s contradictory and obtuse.

Yeah, I agree with that. The ending especially felt like the film didn't know what it wanted to say.

As others have said, the film is critical of Monk and not fully on board with his criticism of "trauma porn," but also, what you're describing isn't trauma porn. It's just drama. Even Monk, who again is kind of a snob, doesn't expect people to write novels where nothing bad happens to black characters, where there's no conflict or hardships to overcome. He would be perfectly fine with novel telling a dramatic story that could just as easily happen to a white character. What he hates is this[urban fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_fiction?wprov=sfla1).

Then there's nothing to imply anything other than the ending is part of the script. Dont think it was that thought through that its a pick and choose what is part of the script and what isn't, and if it is that's a pretty weak defence for the movies parts that don't work for some people eg. family drama. They spend a lot of time on it and none of it seems blatantly awards baity enough to qualify as satirical on the state of the awards / movie culture

This might be antithetical to the point of this whole sub, but here goes: just enjoy the movie, bro. The premise of any film becomes ridiculous if you break it down enough. Like when my wife watched The Godfather for the first time she said, “All of these people should be in prison, why do I care what happens to them?” There is just a little bit of suspension of disbelief and some critical facilities necessary to enjoy a movie.

I fundamentally don't think it's accurate to describe the family drama in the film as "trauma porn" or equivalent to exploitation cinema. It deals with the dynamics of the family, including the trauma aspects, with a fair degree of restraint and poise, and it certainly doesn't centre or play up that trauma for some external audience gratification. A film that depicts trauma or sad events is not necessarily "trauma porn". I would encourage being very judicious in how we use that term in case we end up just making up a thought-terminating cliché of dismissing huge swathes of substantial drama, and I certainly wouldn't describe the drama aspects of the film in that way.
Thank you. The entirety of OP's point seems to be based on the concept that drama in and of itself is somehow a negative.

I don't think the film is communicating the idea that the in-film narrative, while Monk's creation, isn't heavily autobiographical, at least within his perspective. The stuff he is shown to be inventing for the film is all at the end and he is reluctant to do so. It's not a totally unsupported reading but I wouldn't take it as "the point".

The drama half of the movie felt like it hit basically the same tone as The Holdovers, and nobody accused that movie of being white middle-aged schlub trauma porn. A man that needs to open up, dementia, heartfelt conversations, and some good jokes sprinkled in. Maybe you are doing exactly the sorts of things that the movie is complaining audiences do to “black” movies?

To me, it seems as though you’ve misinterpreted wide swaths of not just this film, but the language of cinema.
 
As others have pointed out, I think it’s a misrepresentation to call the family drama in this film “trauma porn.” Would you say the same thing about the white family in May December? Put it another way, if you took out the satire from American Fiction, just focused on the family elements and made the characters white, would you call their drama trauma porn?

Your analysis also ignores the fact that we are very clearly not meant to completely agree with all of Monk’s opinions. When he interacts with Issa Rae’s character, he begrudgingly finds himself agreeing with her opinions and respecting her judgment. He’s also surprised to see how easily she cuts through the bullshit of his book and see how superficial it is. Then we learn that Monk hasn’t even read the book that set him on the path he took. It’s clear that though we are meant to sympathize with Monk’s plight as a black author, we’re also meant to laugh at the clumsy and superficial way in which he dumbs himself down for publishers.

It should also be noted that the book Monk writes isn’t satire, he even says plainly that it’s a “fuck you” to publishers, a way of daring them to sell the dumbest book he could think of writing while pissed drunk. Monk even tries several times to torpedo the book, culminating in him changing the title to “Fuck”. The satire comes from the film’s depiction of how mostly white rooms then take Monk’s book and elevate it far beyond the his intentions and the actual quality of the narrative (which Issa Rae rightly critiques). My favorite scene is when the three white authors select “Fuck” for “Book of the Year” because we “have to listen to black voices” while dismissing the arguments against the book made by the two black authors in the room.
[removed]

The black characters in American Fiction are richly drawn, complex, three dimensional people dealing with myriad life issues, none of which have anything to do with being black. This, of course, is Monk's central point: he doesn't identify by race. He rejects racial essentialism. He continues to adhere to the classical liberal view that we should treat people as individuals, judging them by the content of their characters, and insisting on equal standards equally applied.

The white characters are relentlessly stereotyped -- a group of white Stepin Fetchits presented as performative, virtue signalling, condescending, patronizing identity politics white liberals, but ultimately clowns. The clowns are racial essentialists.

Complex, realistic black characters contrasted against clowning white characters -- ok, that's an inversion of an old Hollywood trope, and fair enough. 

Should we point out the other racial stereotype now in vogue in FilmWorld: the sympathetic, complex, heroic black characters surrounded by racist white characters who are uniformly evil -- unless an heroic white savior character emerges as an ally or protector, but white saviorism is now in disfavor and would probably get a film anathematized. 

Just to round this out, perhaps we should also acknowledge the many movies which, like Monk himself, have essentially moved beyond race, movies in which the white and black characters (not to mention the Hispanic, Asian, Native American, Romulan, Klingon, and Vulcan characters) are simply there, treating each other as people without any regard for race. Those movies are abundant today. In fairness to Hollywood, we should recognize that these films are there. So what is being parodied in American Fiction?

If we transpose from American Fiction to the real world, it should be noted that every white character in the film -- every one of them a clown -- would in the real world almost certainly be a liberal in contemporary U.S. political terms. They are drawn from the worlds of academia, publishing and film, all overwhelmingly LeftWorld in orientation with a handful of conservatives hiding out here and there. 

There are two questions I would like to ask Cord Jefferson. The first is whether he considered the likelihood that RightWorld and LeftWorld audiences will see two essentially different movies. RightWorld audiences will think that American Fiction says exactly what conservatives (the scattering of black conservatives included) have been saying for years about the woke identity politics left. They won't be squirming at the parody; they will be standing up and cheering. Was this Cord Jefferson's intent, or is he so deep in his own silo -- has he ever worked in a reasonably bipartisan or perhaps even conservative dominated space -- that the movie reflects his own blind spot?

This raises a subsidiary question. Did Cord Jefferson ever consider introducing a contrasting white character -- someone mirroring Monk's own views -- to break the clown stereotype? 

One possible example: when Monk first gets crosswise with his department, he might have received a visit from another faculty member offering support. This might be a fellow professor Monk has never met, but of whom he is aware because he is notorious on campus as the lone conservative, maybe even the sole registered Republican in a faculty of 1,236. He has survived several purge attempts because he is very senior, tenured, and well lawyered, and he is smart enough to avoid careless mistakes. He has been handling woke students like the one who got Monk in trouble for years; it's an art form. He is now grudgingly tolerated and gets rolled out every Diversity Day to assure disgruntled alumni that the university is not a complete ideological monoculture. (Of course, he will eventually retire, and the DEI screens on hiring will ensure that he will be the last of his kind.) He knocks on Monk's door, introduces himself, grins, and says, "Welcome to the Resistance."

The loss of ideological and viewpoint diversity is a serious issue. Did Cord Jefferson intend the parody to extend to that subject as well?

I’ll just note. That conversation with the writer (Issa Rae) never takes place in the actual novel, and I think that inclusion did in fact muddy whatever point the adaptation was going for. The novel never really attempts to ‘absolve’ Issa Rae’s character of the shit she’s selling.

I don’t remember the exact phrasing, but when Monk and Coraline argue about the book, he says “my life is a mess, but not like that”. The things he’s experiencing are traumatic, sure, but mundane (a death in the family, an ailing mother, a bad relationship with his brother).

I’ve seen people point out the drama bits are a bit boring, and I agree. That’s what make them work. It’s the banal suffering that permeates our lives contrasting with the historical suffering in stories about black people.

your wife has a point

That scene is gold. I think part of the muted/critical response to this movie in some corners is just white defensiveness. I think another part is difficulty accepting characters as characters, independent of their "blackness," and narrators as fully human and semi-reliable, themes that this movie is trying to explore. That makes the movie all the more relevant and successful imo. 

I think it's an adult movie that isn't telling the audience what to think, but is presenting different perspectives and leaving them there for your consideration. That's not a flaw, but complexity. Audiences seem to be falling all over themselves to praise certain one-note, hamfisted films that are style over substance this year and sleeping on American Fiction, but that is commentary on the audience rather than the films as far as I can tell.

> Would you say the same thing about the white family in May December?

YES. The whole point of the satirical bent of that film (which is found in Natalie Portman's scene where she mimes the rape scene, and then filming it in the end, and in one scene saying all the picks for the child actor aren't "sexy enough') is that the these heartbreaking stories, when turned into entertainment media, are implicitly understood to be partly if not entirely consumed as pornographic trauma. Thanks for making my point for me.

> Put it another way, if you took out the satire from American Fiction, just focused on the family elements and made the characters white, would you call their drama trauma porn?

I don't know if it rises to that level, mainly because it is so uninteresting and shallow, but yes that is what it aspires to be. I mean, two siblings are talking and then one of them suddenly drops dead, the mother develops dementia in the next scene, and the brother becomes a coke addict in the following scene. How is that not trauma porn, regardless of their color, as you say?

Haven't watched it but the vibe I get is "skewering white liberals while seeking validation from white liberals." Basically a kind of POC story that centers the concerns of bourgeois POC and crowds out the experiences of everyday people.
Yeah the whole storyline with the housekeeper was crazy wrong tbh

To add to your point, the movie just also felt outdated? Like, the stereotypical depiction of black people they were criticizing is waaaaaayy less prevalent today than before the way they were implying.

The film is saying that it’s not a black person’s job to educate white liberals on the trials and tribulations of black life. It’s a film about honoring your culture while trying to escape becoming a monolith for other people to project survivor’s guilt onto.
[removed]

>The novel never really attempts to ‘absolve’ Issa Rae’s character of the shit she’s selling. And personally, I don’t think it’s snobbish to critique upper class writers who essentially exploit the narratives of lower class folks who happen to be from their racial demographic.

I agree! 
I felt like all she did in that scene was justify herself, she doesn’t actually challenge his beliefs. She basically accuses him of being an out-of-touch elitist, doesn’t she? I also seem to recall her framing Monk’s criticism as being a man coming after a woman, kinda using identity politics as a shield. But doesn’t she also admit that she’s just giving the white publishers what they want, which is exactly what Monk is accusing her of?
White critics have almost universally hailed it, however. To a degree I think smacks of defensiveness, because (to me) it’s a pretty average and very muddled movie.

The film plays with layers of narrative - the film itself is based on a novel, and the main character writes a novel that is adapted into a film. I think you're intended to see the film itself as one of the layers of the narrative, similar to how it's handled in Adaptation

I don't think it's "guilty" of what it's critiquing so much as including that as a facet of the narrative.

I wasn't thinking of critics at all. It's not getting the love on forums like this and in real life conversations I've had that other nominated films are this year. Where you see muddle I see the complexity of a movie that is operating on multiple levels and isn't telling me what to think, but is asking me to think. It's the kind of movie where the viewer has to do some of the work.

I agree with your questions. When reflecting on the film earlier, here is something I wrote on letterboxd that relates to your comment:

“While Monk deliberately wrote to insult his readers, Sintara paddles a grift dressed up in the language of empowerment and representation, and there is a soft suggestion that this makes a difference. Sintara highlights how little Monk thinks of his own culture, and while it’s true that he is racially alienated, Sinatra isn’t the cultural ambassador she makes herself out to be so much as an opportunist.”

It’s harsh but that’s basically my interpretation of the conversation. It unnecessarily set up her character as this easy, proud foil to Monk’s insecurities. It just removed nuance imo. It’s possible to highlight Monk’s “flaws” without valorizing the other author.
Yes, it was way over the top and not subtle at all. Not everything has to be subtle, of course, but this was just too much.

Others have said something similar, but the novel Erasure that the film is based on mentions early on that while Monk is unquestionably black, he doesn't beat any of the stereotypical markers of being black.Frim the book's perspective, Monk just happens to be black.So his trauma is family trauma that just happens to be black family trauma.

The book is about the possibility of creating art within a restrictive sphere of production that doesn't allow black artists to be anything other than BLACK artists, which is also why Monk writes My Pafology as a satire of Native Son
Yeah agreed. If it's gonna be over the top it has to actually be funny, not cringe. I still enjoyed the movie tbh but that part brought it down.

The whole housekeeper romance subplot is cliched and superfluous. 

The mom-going-gaga stuff is dull and formulaic. 

The literary-award subplot is never properly integrated. And the final conversation with Issa Rae’s character shows the film trying to have it both ways. 

The Player-like ending feels like the work of someone who hasn’t worked out how to end their story. 

Jefferson’s blocking of scenes and shot-composition is strictly TV-movie level. (Especially the drone establishing shots of the seaside town. 🤢)

Unless you’re really into Waiting Room Jazz, the score sucks. 

. . . So, yeah. I don’t mind being asked to do some of the work, but it has to be in the service of something a lot more accomplished than this.

>And by trauma porn, for everyone's edification, is just having characters wallowing in misery with no hope, or exploiting wounds to milk tears and sympathies out of the audience without providing anything else.

Either you didn't watch the movie or you're ignoring how it contradicts with your own definition. How can you say there's no hope? Monk reconnects with his sister before her death. He reconnects with his brother, who makes progress in coming to terms with his sexuality and how it affects his relationship to his parents. They find a safe place for their mother to live, using Monk's book money to solve their financial hardships. Does everything have to be completely perfect at the end for it to count as a movie with hope?

The ending kind of contradicts this reading, though. He sells out, giving the white director the ending he wants. When he goes out to the studio lot he acknowledges the actor playing a slave in the director's current production. In a way, he reconciled with the role the industry has given him. However, it's not really played as if this is some sort of moral failure. It shows that he has become more pragmatic, moving closer to the point of view of the Issa Rae's character. He no longer blames black artists for perpetuating certain types of stories. Another person replied to me that it's different in the novel. But the way it plays out in the movie is contradictory.

The housekeeper romance shows two frumpy middle aged characters finding love, something rarely (if ever) represented for audiences. The movie in general shows characters meeting the challenges of middle age, something as a culture we're not very interested in looking into to, because it isn't sexy and doesn't sell. I appreciated that this movie decided to buck that trend and look there. 

I'm sorry that a mother losing her memory was boring to you. Have you had that experience? Have you considered that that might be something that many people are going through or have gone through, and it is complicated and difficult and underrepresented in film given how universal a human experience it is? Sorry it wasn't catered to you specifically and didn't work for you, but it is relatable, and the source of much emotion, to many older people. 

That conversation with her is where maybe you're seeing muddle and I'm seeing that it's possible for different characters to have differing perspectives because of where they're coming from, each character having valid reasons for their respective and therefore neither is wrong nor right and when they confront each other that is the bedrock of actual dialogue. It reminds me of the F. Scott Fitzgerald quote that "the test of a first-rate intelligence is the ability to hold two opposing ideas in mind at the same time and still retain the ability to function." I think American Fiction operates in this space, to its credit. It also asks the audience to go there, to mixed results. 

I think style-wise, I agree with you, but I also don't think that's where it's trying to succeed, which I found refreshing, since many other nominated films are the opposite: they use stylistic flourishes and technical proficiency to mask the fact that they don't have much to say.

I thought it was strange, too, that Monk’s girlfriend read and enjoyed his novel, much to Monk’s dismay. The movie kind of just leaves this hanging, but I really thought an interrogation of this exact phenomenon would benefit the movie’s point immensely. This is the “causal consumer” so to speak, a black woman just looking for some light reading, and she inadvertently enjoys something that Monk wrote to diss other black authors. Is this “problematic” or not? The movie doesn’t seem interested in answering this, it gives that interrogation to Issa Rae’s character instead, and she just comes off sounding like an enormous hypocrite.

How is Issa Rae’s character not guilty of the exact same thing Monk is? Granted, Monk did not read her entire novel, but based on that excerpt we’re given, it’s clear that it is the exact type of novel that “Fuck” is but written completely sincerely.

i don’t think it’s contradictory at all. everything you described is also how i read it, except i feel that the film is willing to acknowledge that there’s no perfect answer to this problem. i dont understand what’s contradictory about it. the film does not have a happy ending and it doesn’t claim to have all of the answers. 

ultimately we wind up where we started, because the protagonist still feels uncomfortable with his position as a successful, well-educated black man in a country full of white liberals who wants to find sob stories in his culture’s history, and while issa is more comfortable with where she “came from”, jeffery is not, and he doesn’t want to acknowledge it. it’s an issue that winds up transcending race, and falls more into class, and again, survivor’s guilt.
...You think a good critique of The Godfather is 'I shouldn't care about any of these people since they should be in jail' ?

I mean, did you miss the entire scene where the movie quite literally addresses this point? Monk confronts her about it and she talks about how she spent years doing interviews and research for her book. Despite how it may appear, it was a sincere and authentic portrayal of real people her character encountered. She also admits that she wrote for the market but disagrees with Monk (and maybe the viewer) about whether or not that's a bad thing.

I think it's crazy that you would define trauma porn as "having characters wallowing in misery with no hope, or exploiting wounds to milk tears and sympathies out of the audience without providing anything else" when neither this film nor May December fit that definition. 

American Fiction is a satirical comedy, the "trauma" that Monk experiences - the death of a sister, a mother going through dementia, and struggling financially - are not things that leave him "wallowing in misery." May December is also not so much "trauma porn" as a commentary on how the entertainment industry exploits the stories of people who have gone through traumatic events. It also doesn't have characters "wallowing in misery" as much as they are just living their lives, trying their best to cope with the decisions they've made.

Again, it seems like you have some fundamental misunderstandings about the language of cinema.

There’s a foundational flaw in your analysis, which is describing a relatively normal family drama as “trauma porn”, which it isn’t, and then citing films like Get Out, which arguably is closer to it, if not totally so. Generally speaking, trauma porn is exploiting tragedy into spectacle, for the sake of enticing an audience. The most tragic part of the movie happens off screen, before the events of the film, and is not really loaded with any kind of cultural context, and exists more as thematic support for the Wright and Brown’s characters than being any kind of point in of itself. 

Mind you, I don’t necessarily think that your premise is inherently flawed though. I thought American Fiction was great, and part of why I thought it worked so well was that it allowed nuance and implication to carry the narrative through out of its own danger zone. But I do think it’s very much both a commentary that is, in many ways, just like a handful of years late and simultaneously trailblazing a way through for new “white liberal” appeal. I wouldn’t necessarily hold its critical appeal and awards success against it, of course, but I definitely think it’s hilariously ironic in that regard.

I’m not buying it, sorry. The movie is telling you that Issa’s book is different (because it’s “well researched”?) without actually showing you how, but then she blatantly admits that she is pandering to the market. This isn’t virtuous, it’s no different than what Monk is doing.

Other people have said all the right things. I just want to add one aspect that’s often overlooked and that you definitely overlooked.

The movie spends a long time having us agree with Monk’s critique of Black stereotypes in literature and film. His conversation with Issa Rae feels justified and noble. Until the very end. When she points out that you only see potential in what you don’t think is good enough.

We cut from that to Monk by himself, sending an apology text to Coraline. It’s a moment where he’s humbled enough to finally reach out. WHAT’S IMPORTANT IS THE VISUAL AT THE END. Monk looks over and sees a shot of a Black child being shown two dolls, one white, one Black. Monk spends  a few seconds taking in the picture. 

The picture is famous. It’s from a study known as the Doll Test, conducted in the 40s and 50s.

> Drs. Clark used four dolls, identical except for color, to test children’s racial perceptions. Their subjects, children between the ages of three to seven, were asked to identify both the race of the dolls and which color doll they prefer. A majority of the children preferred the white doll and assigned positive characteristics to it. The Clarks concluded that “prejudice, discrimination, and segregation” created a feeling of inferiority among African-American children and damaged their self-esteem. 

The picture isn’t a coincidence. It’s the film acknowledging that Monk’s position had been fueled by self-loathing. Which is why he ultimately makes the movie. He’s trying to find a middle ground between Issa Rae and his own previous views.

So even if the family drama was “guilty” of the the meta-story’s criticism, that’s fine because the meta-story was actually an incorrect position.

[For an entire thematic, literary breakdown of the movie](https://filmcolossus.com/american-fiction-2023-explained)

Again, I think you missed the entire point of that scene and the character's interactions leading up to it. Monk was "offended" by the fact that Issa Rae's book was being praised and did so well, but he never even took the time to read it. As such, he doesn't have any idea about any sort of meaningful depth the story may or may not have had. Since Monk is our defacto narrator, it also deprives the viewer from knowing as well.

We also see Monk repeatedly being surprised with or agreeing with points that Issa Rae's character makes not just about "Fuck" but on a wide range of issues that come up among the judges of the literary contest. Issa's character goes from being a one-note antagonist to a three-dimensional character with depth, intelligence and salient opinions.

And at no point did Issa Rae claim any sort of virtue. She's a writer trying to make a living. And as she said, just because she's well educated, connected and working at a major publishing house doesn't mean she's not allowed to explore stories of racial and class struggle and make money of what the market is asking for.
>THIS THING <BAD ADJECTIVE>. THIS THING <BAD ADJECTIVE>. THIS THING <COMPARISON TO SOMETHING BAD>. THIS THING <BAD ADJECTIVE>.
Issa's character is at least doing it in good faith and not doing it as a mockery in the same way Monk is. They're not doing to same thing.

You know, I caught a whiff of that thought, undercutting my joy in the movie, I saw myself as that woman who completely doesn't get it, and then no, that doesn't defeat my joy in the movie, and sure the heart strings are tugged at, but that's part of the story of a man who is quite brilliant, regardless of race, and has quite a fantastic family, and maybe class or even gayness are more oppressive. It's a story about the things that inhibit your from expressing your true self, and race is perhaps a big part of it even if you deny it, the question was could he express who he really was. I thought the horror of the movie was that he was playing a trick on people, he was mocking blacksploitation and using it to fund his mother's care, ends justify the means, and what's the difference between pandering and giving the audience the catharsis they want because you love life? I really wished he could talk about how he meant to make fun of people, and that enriched him, and then his disclosure impoverished him, led to hard choices, that would have been my ending. I think it was too far into the movie to have those revelations, and so the easy multiple outs by framing it as a screenplay. I thought up to that point the movie had integrity, and I don't begrudge them that ending either. I mean I thought it was better than the usual making fun of hollywood by doing all the hollywood tricks (Babylon or Showgirls).

>And personally, I don’t think it’s snobbish to critique upper class writers who essentially exploit the narratives of lower class folks who happen to be from their racial demographic.

I think the part that people are missing is that Monk wasn't engaging in a good faith critique of Sintara's work. He never read it. He saw the excerpt reading and immediately wrote it off as stereotypical trash that didn't deserve the success it got.
